meta.titre: Protecting Information: threats, security measures and the rights of data subjects
meta.sous_theme: Security measures and data protection principles

sections.contenu_markdown: A mobile-money agent in Douala writes customers' phone numbers and balances in a notebook, and a clinic in Bamenda keeps patient files on one shared computer. If the notebook is stolen, or an employee copies the files, real people can be harmed even though no equipment is broken. Examination questions on this theme ask you to name a protective measure, explain how it works and say what it protects. For personal data they also ask what a person may expect from the organisation that holds it.

items: A network connects computers so that they can share data and devices, and the Internet is a network of networks.
Data are raw facts, and information is data that has been processed so that it has meaning.
A database stores records about people, such as patients or customers, in tables.

sections.titre: Threats, security measures and data protection principles
sections.contenu_markdown:
### The three aims of security
Information security protects three properties of data. **Confidentiality**: only authorised people can read it. **Integrity**: it stays accurate and is not changed without authority. **Availability**: authorised users can reach it when they need it. **Privacy** is the right of a person to control how data about them is collected, used and shared. **Data security** is the set of technical and physical measures that makes privacy possible.

### Threats
| Threat | Example | Aim harmed |
|---|---|---|
| Unauthorised access (hacking) | an outsider guesses a weak password | confidentiality |
| Malware | a virus deletes or locks files | integrity and availability |
| Phishing | a fake e-mail asks the user to type a password | confidentiality |
| Human error | a file is deleted by mistake | integrity and availability |
| Theft or physical damage | stolen laptop, fire, flood, power surge | all three |
| Misuse by an insider | an employee copies customer data | confidentiality |

### Security measures
| Measure | How it works | Main protection |
|---|---|---|
| Passwords and authentication | a strong password is long and mixes letters, digits and symbols; two-factor authentication needs two different kinds of proof, such as something known and something owned | unauthorised access |
| Access rights | each user receives only the permissions needed (read only, edit, delete) | insider misuse, human error |
| Firewall | hardware or software that checks traffic between a private network and an outside network and blocks what breaks its rules | intrusion from the network |
| Anti-malware and updates | scans files for known malicious code; patches close weaknesses | malware |
| Encryption | turns plaintext into ciphertext with an algorithm and a key | reading of stolen or intercepted data |
| Backup | copies kept on another device or at another site | loss of data (availability) |
| Physical controls | locked rooms, ID cards, biometric locks, a UPS against power cuts | theft, damage, power loss |
| Audit trail | a log of who opened or changed what | deters misuse and gives evidence |

### Data protection principles
A responsible organisation collects personal data for a stated purpose, collects only what is relevant, keeps it accurate, keeps it no longer than needed, keeps it secure, and does not pass it to others without consent or a legal reason. The person the data is about (the **data subject**) can expect to be told that data is held, to see it, to have wrong data corrected and to object to uses they did not agree to. Laws differ between countries, so state the principle in your answer and do not quote an article of law.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question names a situation and asks for measures.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Write each measure as three parts: the measure, how it works, and what it protects in that situation. A bare word such as "passwords" earns little. Match the measure to the threat in the scenario: a clinic with a network connection needs a firewall and access rights, a shop with one computer needs backup and physical locks.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to compare ways of encrypting.
variantes.contenu_markdown: With **symmetric** encryption the same key encrypts and decrypts, so it is fast but the key must be shared safely. With **asymmetric** encryption there is a public key and a private key: anyone may use the public key to encrypt a message for you, and only your private key decrypts it, so no secret key has to be sent. A **shift cipher** replaces each letter by the letter a fixed number of places later (wrapping from Z to A). It is easy to break because there are only 25 useful keys and letter frequencies remain visible.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked how long a password takes to find by trial.
variantes.contenu_markdown: The number of possible passwords is (number of allowed characters) raised to the power (length). Six lowercase letters give $26^6 = 308\,915\,776$ possibilities. Longer length and a larger character set multiply the work of a guessing program. The worst-case time is the number of possibilities divided by the number of guesses per second.

sections.enonce_markdown: A private clinic in Bafoussam stores patient records on a server that is connected to the Internet. (a) Describe THREE measures the clinic should use to protect the records. [6 marks] (b) State TWO rights that a patient should have over the personal data held about him or her. [2 marks]

etapes.action: Read the command words and the marks.
etapes.justification: "Describe" asks for what the measure is and how it works, and six marks for three measures means two marks each.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Three developed measures, each with a measure and a reason; two named rights.

etapes.action: Identify the threats in the scenario.
etapes.justification: The server is on the Internet and holds sensitive data, so outsiders, malware and careless staff are all risks.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Threats: hacking, malware, misuse by staff, loss of data.

etapes.action: Choose three measures that match these threats.
etapes.justification: Each measure must answer a threat that you can name.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Firewall (network intrusion), access rights with passwords (misuse), encryption or backup (readability and loss).

etapes.action: Develop each measure into a full sentence with its effect.
etapes.justification: The mark is for the working of the measure, not only its name.
etapes.resultat_markdown: See the model answer in the conclusion.

etapes.action: Answer part (b) with rights, not with security measures.
etapes.justification: A right is something the patient may expect from the clinic.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Right to see the data held; right to have wrong data corrected.

sections.conclusion_markdown:
**(a)** A **firewall** is placed between the clinic's network and the Internet and blocks incoming traffic that does not follow its rules, so outsiders cannot reach the server. **Access rights** give each member of staff only the permissions needed, protected by individual passwords, so a receptionist can see appointments but cannot change a diagnosis, which limits misuse and mistakes. **Encryption** of the stored records turns them into ciphertext, so that a stolen disk cannot be read without the key. (A regular **backup** kept at another site would also be accepted, because it allows the records to be restored after loss.)

**(b)** The patient may see the information held about him or her, and may have inaccurate information corrected.

items.erreur_markdown: "A firewall protects the computer from viruses."
items.pourquoi_faux: A firewall filters network traffic by rules. Finding and removing malicious code in files is the job of anti-malware software.
items.correction_markdown: A firewall blocks unauthorised network connections; anti-malware software detects and removes malware.

items.erreur_markdown: "Data security and data privacy mean the same thing."
items.pourquoi_faux: Privacy is about the person's control over their data. Security is the set of measures that protects the data from loss and unauthorised access.
items.correction_markdown: Security measures (passwords, encryption) help to deliver privacy, but privacy also needs rules about purpose, accuracy and disclosure.

items.erreur_markdown: "Backups stop hackers from getting into the system."
items.pourquoi_faux: A backup does not prevent access. It only allows lost or damaged data to be restored.
items.correction_markdown: Backups protect availability and integrity after a loss. To prevent access use a firewall, access rights and strong authentication.

items.erreur_markdown: "Encryption stops the data from being stolen."
items.pourquoi_faux: Encrypted data can still be copied. Encryption makes the copy unreadable to someone who does not have the key.
items.correction_markdown: Encryption protects confidentiality of data that has been stolen or intercepted; other measures reduce the chance of theft.

items.erreur_markdown: Answering "Name one security measure" with "passwords" and nothing else.
items.pourquoi_faux: The mark scheme rewards how the measure works and what it protects; a single word earns little.
items.correction_markdown: A password is a secret string typed by the user to prove identity, so that only authorised users can open the system.

items.enonce_markdown: Define confidentiality, integrity and availability. For each of them give ONE threat that harms it.
items.solution_markdown:
Award a mark for each correct definition and each matched threat.

- **Confidentiality**: only authorised people can read the data. Threat: a hacker or a dishonest employee copying the data.
- **Integrity**: the data stays accurate and is changed only with authority. Threat: malware that alters records, or a user who overwrites a file by mistake.
- **Availability**: authorised users can reach the data when needed. Threat: a fire, a power failure or a virus that makes files unusable.

**Three definitions, each with one matched threat.**

items.enonce_markdown: A trader in a market in Mbouda hides the prices she pays suppliers with a shift cipher of key 4: every letter is replaced by the letter four places later in the alphabet, and Z is followed by A. (a) Encrypt the word MARKET. (b) She writes the word WXSGO in her book. Decrypt it. (c) Give ONE reason why this cipher gives weak protection.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Move each letter four places on: M to Q, A to E, R to V, K to O, E to I, T to X. The ciphertext is **QEVOIX**.

(b) Move each letter four places back: W to S, X to T, S to O, G to C, O to K. The plaintext is **STOCK**.

(c) There are only 25 useful keys, so all of them can be tried quickly, and the frequency of letters in a language still shows through. Award a mark for either reason.

items.enonce_markdown: A school office protects its computer with a password made only of lowercase letters. (a) A password has 6 characters. How many different passwords are possible? (b) A program tests 1 000 passwords every second. Give the longest time it would need, in hours to one decimal place. (c) The school changes the rule to 6 characters chosen from 26 lowercase letters, 26 capitals and 10 digits. How many times more passwords are possible than in (a), to the nearest whole number? (d) The office takes a full backup of 40 GB every Sunday and an incremental backup of 2 GB on each of the other six days, and keeps four weeks of backups. How much storage is needed?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) 26 choices for each of 6 positions: $26^6 = $ **308\,915\,776** passwords.

(b) Longest time (every possibility tested) $= 308\,915\,776 \div 1000 = 308\,915.776$ s. Divide by 3600: $308\,915.776 \div 3600 = $ **85.8 hours** (to one decimal place).

(c) The character set has $26 + 26 + 10 = 62$ characters, so $62^6 = 56\,800\,235\,584$ passwords. The ratio is $56\,800\,235\,584 \div 308\,915\,776 \approx 183.9$, so there are about **184 times** more passwords.

(d) Each week: one full backup (40 GB) and six incremental backups ($6 \times 2 = 12$ GB), that is 52 GB. Four weeks: $4 \times 52 = $ **208 GB**.

items_markdown: Security protects confidentiality, integrity and availability; privacy is the person's control over data about them.
Answer a measure question in three parts: the measure, how it works, what it protects.
A firewall filters network traffic; anti-malware removes malicious code; they do different jobs.
Encryption does not stop theft but makes stolen data unreadable without the key; a backup does not stop access but allows recovery.
Number of possible passwords = characters allowed to the power of length, and longer passwords with more character types take far longer to guess.
A data subject can expect to be told about, to see and to have corrected the data held about them, and the data must be kept secure.
